claim: African weakly electric fishes (Mormyroidea) evolved a mosaically enlarged cerebellum and hindbrain.
source: African weakly electric fishes (Mormyroidea) evolved a mosaically enlarged cerebellum and hindbrain, yet the relationship to their behaviorally novel electrosensory system remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding from previous research.

claim: South American weakly electric fishes (Gymnotiformes) and weakly electric catfishes (Synodontis spp.) evolved electrosensory systems independent of mormyroids.
source: We addressed this by studying South American weakly electric fishes (Gymnotiformes) and weakly electric catfishes (Synodontis spp.), which evolved varying aspects of electrosensory systems, independent of mormyroids.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: All three electrogenic lineages show mosaic increases in cerebellum relative to non-electric lineages.
source: We found mosaic increases in cerebellum in all three electrogenic lineages relative to non-electric lineages and mosaic increases in torus semicircularis and hindbrain associated with the evolution of electrogenesis and electroreceptor type.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analyses presented in the Results section.

claim: Mosaic increases in torus semicircularis and hindbrain are associated with the evolution of electrogenesis and electroreceptor type.
source: We found mosaic increases in cerebellum in all three electrogenic lineages relative to non-electric lineages and mosaic increases in torus semicircularis and hindbrain associated with the evolution of electrogenesis and electroreceptor type.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analyses in the Results section.

claim: Evolving novel electrosensory systems is repeatedly and independently associated with changes in the sizes of individual major brain regions independent of brain size.
source: These results show that evolving novel electrosensory systems is repeatedly and independently associated with changes in the sizes of individual major brain regions independent of brain size, suggesting that selection can impact structural brain composition to favor specific regions involved in novel behaviors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the findings from the study.

claim: Selection can impact structural brain composition to favor specific regions involved in novel behaviors.
source: These results show that evolving novel electrosensory systems is repeatedly and independently associated with changes in the sizes of individual major brain regions independent of brain size, suggesting that selection can impact structural brain composition to favor specific regions involved in novel behaviors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Brain region size generally scales allometrically with brain size.
source: Brain region size generally scales allometrically with brain size, but mosaic shifts in brain region size independent of brain size have been found in several lineages and may be related to the evolution of behavioral novelty.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Mosaic shifts in brain region size independent of brain size have been found in several lineages.
source: Brain region size generally scales allometrically with brain size, but mosaic shifts in brain region size independent of brain size have been found in several lineages and may be related to the evolution of behavioral novelty.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Mosaic shifts in brain region size may be related to the evolution of behavioral novelty.
source: Brain region size generally scales allometrically with brain size, but mosaic shifts in brain region size independent of brain size have been found in several lineages and may be related to the evolution of behavioral novelty.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the abstract based on existing literature.

claim: Much of the variation in brain region sizes is attributed to the allometric scaling of each region with total brain size (concerted evolution).
source: Much of the variation in brain region sizes is attributed to the allometric scaling of each region with total brain size (concerted evolution), which may result from conservation and constraint in developmental neurogenesis (Finlay and Darlington, 1995; Striedter, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Concerted evolution may result from conservation and constraint in developmental neurogenesis.
source: Much of the variation in brain region sizes is attributed to the allometric scaling of each region with total brain size (concerted evolution), which may result from conservation and constraint in developmental neurogenesis (Finlay and Darlington, 1995; Striedter, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous research.

claim: Seemingly disproportionately enlarged regions can have larger allometric slopes by extending the timing of neurogenesis for late developing brain regions such as the cortex and cerebellum.
source: Seemingly disproportionately enlarged regions can have larger allometric slopes by extending the timing of neurogenesis for late developing brain regions such as the cortex and cerebellum (Finlay and Darlington, 1995).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Changes in brain region sizes independent of total brain size, or mosaic shifts, have been observed in several taxa.
source: However, changes in brain region sizes independent of total brain size, or mosaic shifts, have also been observed in several taxa and are hypothesized to reflect selection on traits associated with those regions (Barton and Harvey, 2000; Striedter, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Mosaic shifts are hypothesized to reflect selection on traits associated with those regions.
source: However, changes in brain region sizes independent of total brain size, or mosaic shifts, have also been observed in several taxa and are hypothesized to reflect selection on traits associated with those regions (Barton and Harvey, 2000; Striedter, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with supporting citations.

claim: Mosaic shifts in fine-scale brain regions and circuits are well accepted and have been linked to changes in behavior.
source: Mosaic shifts in fine-scale brain regions and circuits are well accepted and have been linked to changes in behavior (Carlson et al., 2011; Vélez et al., 2017; Vélez et al., 2019; Gutiérrez-Ibáñez et al., 2014; Moore and DeVoogd, 2017; DeCasien and Higham, 2019; Krebs, 1990), but the scale at which selection can act to alter brain region sizes remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The scale at which selection can act to alter brain region sizes remains unclear.
source: Mosaic shifts in fine-scale brain regions and circuits are well accepted and have been linked to changes in behavior (Carlson et al., 2011; Vélez et al., 2017; Vélez et al., 2019; Gutiérrez-Ibáñez et al., 2014; Moore and DeVoogd, 2017; DeCasien and Higham, 2019; Krebs, 1990), but the scale at which selection can act to alter brain region sizes remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: There may be more flexibility for mosaic changes in nuclei or circuits dedicated to specific functions compared to major brain regions that serve multiple functions.
source: There may potentially be more flexibility for mosaic changes in nuclei or circuits dedicated to specific functions compared to major brain regions that serve multiple functions and may be subject to greater developmental and phylogenetic constraints.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction.

claim: Most studies looking at the scaling of major brain regions find evidence of concerted evolution.
source: Most studies looking at the scaling of major brain regions instead find evidence of concerted evolution (Finlay and Darlington, 1995; Striedter, 2005; Yopak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: There is some evidence of mosaic evolution at the scale of major brain regions.
source: There is some evidence of mosaic evolution at these scales (Hoops et al., 2017; Sukhum et al., 2018), but the drivers and selective pressures necessary for mosaic evolution to overcome constraints, whether developmental or due to functional interconnectivity, remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The drivers and selective pressures necessary for mosaic evolution to overcome constraints remain unclear.
source: There is some evidence of mosaic evolution at these scales (Hoops et al., 2017; Sukhum et al., 2018), but the drivers and selective pressures necessary for mosaic evolution to overcome constraints, whether developmental or due to functional interconnectivity, remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Mosaic brain evolution of major brain regions is hypothesized to occur more frequently at larger taxonomic scales and alongside behavioral innovations that open new niches.
source: Mosaic brain evolution of major brain regions is hypothesized to occur more frequently at larger taxonomic scales and alongside behavioral innovations that open new niches since mosaic shifts are more likely to contribute to major differences in brain function (Striedter, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with a supporting citation.

claim: In dragon lizards, mosaic brain evolution is associated with ecomorph.
source: In dragon lizards, mosaic brain evolution is associated with ecomorph (species similar in morphology and behavior inhabiting the same ecological niche; Hoops et al., 2017), but as many different behavioral and sensory changes occur alongside ecomorph development, it is difficult to identify specific selective pressures favoring the observed ecomorph brain structure.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Weakly electric fishes are excellent for testing whether mosaic brain evolution occurs with behavioral novelty.
source: Weakly electric fishes are excellent for testing whether mosaic brain evolution occurs with behavioral novelty: these fishes evolved behaviorally novel active electrosensory systems with several neural innovations, which likely resulted in strong selection for electrosensory processing capabilities (Carlson and Arnegard, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the study with a supporting citation.

claim: Weakly electric fishes evolved behaviorally novel active electrosensory systems with several neural innovations.
source: Weakly electric fishes are excellent for testing whether mosaic brain evolution occurs with behavioral novelty: these fishes evolved behaviorally novel active electrosensory systems with several neural innovations, which likely resulted in strong selection for electrosensory processing capabilities (Carlson and Arnegard, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The evolution of active electrosensory systems in weakly electric fishes likely resulted in strong selection for electrosensory processing capabilities.
source: Weakly electric fishes are excellent for testing whether mosaic brain evolution occurs with behavioral novelty: these fishes evolved behaviorally novel active electrosensory systems with several neural innovations, which likely resulted in strong selection for electrosensory processing capabilities (Carlson and Arnegard, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as an inference with a supporting citation.

claim: Multiple lineages independently evolved similar electrosensory systems.
source: Further, multiple lineages independently evolved similar electrosensory systems (Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Previous studies found that African weakly electric fishes (Mormyroidea) evolved extremely large brains along with mosaic increases in the sizes of the cerebellum and hindbrain relative to other non-electric osteoglossiforms.
source: Previous studies found that African weakly electric fishes (Mormyroidea) evolved extremely large brains along with mosaic increases in the sizes of the cerebellum and hindbrain relative to other non-electric osteoglossiforms (Sukhum et al., 2018; Sukhum et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous research.

claim: The mosaic increases in mormyroids occurred alongside the evolution of an active electrosensory system.
source: These mosaic increases occurred alongside the evolution of an active electrosensory system (electrogenesis + electroreception), but since this is only a single lineage, it is impossible to determine whether these mosaic shifts are associated with the evolution of this electrosensory system or with other phenotypes that differentiate mormyroids from their closest living relatives.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from previous research.

claim: Since mormyroids are only a single lineage, it is impossible to determine whether mosaic shifts are associated with the evolution of the electrosensory system or with other phenotypes.
source: These mosaic increases occurred alongside the evolution of an active electrosensory system (electrogenesis + electroreception), but since this is only a single lineage, it is impossible to determine whether these mosaic shifts are associated with the evolution of this electrosensory system or with other phenotypes that differentiate mormyroids from their closest living relatives.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous research and a rationale for the current study.

claim: Xenomystus nigri is electroreceptive.
source: Further, one non-electric osteoglossiform, Xenomystus nigri, is electroreceptive, and there is no evidence that it has experienced mosaic brain evolution compared to other non-electric osteoglossiforms.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact.

claim: There is no evidence that Xenomystus nigri has experienced mosaic brain evolution compared to other non-electric osteoglossiforms.
source: Further, one non-electric osteoglossiform, Xenomystus nigri, is electroreceptive, and there is no evidence that it has experienced mosaic brain evolution compared to other non-electric osteoglossiforms.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study or previous research.

claim: Electrogenesis and electroreception have evolved at least six times and at least two times, respectively, within ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii).
source: Electrogenesis and electroreception have evolved multiple times, but sparingly, across vertebrates—at least six times and at least two times, respectively, within ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The degree to which electrosensory systems have evolved varies across different independent origins.
source: However, the degree to which electrosensory systems have evolved, with respect to their component parts and how they are utilized, varies across these different independent origins.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: Some lineages produce strong electrical discharges while others produce weak electrical discharges.
source: For example, some lineages produce strong electrical discharges while others produce weak electrical discharges, some lineages have evolved multiple types of electroreceptors while others have evolved just one, and the usage and developmental origins of electrogenesis differ across lineages (Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Some lineages have evolved multiple types of electroreceptors while others have evolved just one.
source: For example, some lineages produce strong electrical discharges while others produce weak electrical discharges, some lineages have evolved multiple types of electroreceptors while others have evolved just one, and the usage and developmental origins of electrogenesis differ across lineages (Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The usage and developmental origins of electrogenesis differ across lineages.
source: For example, some lineages produce strong electrical discharges while others produce weak electrical discharges, some lineages have evolved multiple types of electroreceptors while others have evolved just one, and the usage and developmental origins of electrogenesis differ across lineages (Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Osteoglossiform and otophysan lineages have convergently evolved similar electrosensory systems.
source: Although osteoglossiform and otophysan lineages have convergently evolved similar electrosensory systems (Crampton, 2019), there are some distinctive differences in the degree of electrosensory usage, electroreceptor type, and electrical discharge type that could indicate differential selective pressures on the brains of these species.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: There are distinctive differences in the degree of electrosensory usage, electroreceptor type, and electrical discharge type between osteoglossiform and otophysan lineages.
source: Although osteoglossiform and otophysan lineages have convergently evolved similar electrosensory systems (Crampton, 2019), there are some distinctive differences in the degree of electrosensory usage, electroreceptor type, and electrical discharge type that could indicate differential selective pressures on the brains of these species.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The study combined published osteoglossiform data with otophysan data for a total of 32 species.
source: Using micro-computed tomography (μCT) scans, we measured total brain and brain region volumes for 15 electrogenic, 3 electroreceptive, and 4 non-electrosensory otophysan species. Combined with the published osteoglossiform data, this yielded a dataset of 32 species (Figure 2, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The study measured the volumes of seven distinct brain regions.
source: We measured the volumes of seven distinct brain regions (olfactory bulbs, OB; telencephalon, TEL; hindbrain, HB; optic tectum, OT; torus semicircularis, TS; cerebellum, CB; and rest of brain, RoB) to determine patterns of major brain region scaling across taxa.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Rest of brain includes thalamus, hypothalamus, and additional midbrain structures excluding optic tectum and torus semicircularis.
source: Rest of brain includes thalamus, hypothalamus, and additional midbrain structures excluding optic tectum and torus semicircularis (see 'Brain region delimitation').
evidence: This is stated as a definition in the Results section.

claim: A recent study found a steeper brain–body allometric relationship for osteoglossiforms compared to other actinopterygians.
source: A recent study found a steeper brain–body allometric relationship for osteoglossiforms compared to other actinopterygians, but not for seven other focal ray-finned fish orders, which may, in part, be driven by the highly speciose mormyroids (Tsuboi, 2021).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The study combined brain and body mass data across ray-finned fishes for a total of 870 species across 46 orders.
source: To determine if the evolution of an electrosensory system is associated with extreme encephalization or shifts in brain–body allometric relationships, we combined our data with published brain and body mass data across ray-finned fishes (Tsuboi, 2021; Tsuboi et al., 2018), which resulted in a combined dataset of 870 species across 46 orders, with phylogenetic data from a previously assembled time-calibrated phylogeny (Rabosky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The study identified eight allometric shifts across actinopterygians.
source: We identified eight allometric shifts across actinopterygians, three in lineages with at least three descendants: osteoglossiforms, and two shifts within percomorphs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: All grades differ significantly in slope.
source: We found that all of the grades differ significantly in slope (p<0.05) while only osteoglossiforms relative to the ancestral grade and relative to percomorph grades A and B differ in y-intercept (p<0.05; Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Only osteoglossiforms relative to the ancestral grade and relative to percomorph grades A and B differ in y-intercept.
source: We found that all of the grades differ significantly in slope (p<0.05) while only osteoglossiforms relative to the ancestral grade and relative to percomorph grades A and B differ in y-intercept (p<0.05; Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Only osteoglossiforms had an increased slope relative to the ancestral grade.
source: However, only osteoglossiforms had an increased slope relative to the ancestral grade while the slope for percomorph grade A decreased relative to the ancestral grade with a further decrease in percomorph grade B.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The slope for percomorph grade A decreased relative to the ancestral grade with a further decrease in percomorph grade B.
source: However, only osteoglossiforms had an increased slope relative to the ancestral grade while the slope for percomorph grade A decreased relative to the ancestral grade with a further decrease in percomorph grade B.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The model with eight shifts provided the best fit to the data.
source: We found that the model with eight shifts provided the best fit to the data (2ln(BF)>28; Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Fishes can evolve an active electrosensory system without evolving a brain as large as that of mormyroids.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that fishes can evolve an active electrosensory system without evolving a brain as large as that of mormyroids.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section.

claim: Electrogenic species cluster distinctly from both electroreceptive and non-electrosensory species in the pPCA.
source: We found that electrogenic species cluster distinctly from both electroreceptive and non-electrosensory species, which overlap considerably (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Electroreceptive and non-electrosensory species overlap considerably in the pPCA.
source: We found that electrogenic species cluster distinctly from both electroreceptive and non-electrosensory species, which overlap considerably (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: All electroreceptive lineages have evolved ampullary electroreceptors.
source: All electroreceptive lineages (mormyroids, Xenomystus, gymnotiforms, and siluriforms) have evolved ampullary electroreceptors, which detect relatively low-frequency electrical information, while only gymnotiforms and mormyroids have evolved additional tuberous electroreceptors that broaden the frequency range of detectable signals (Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Ampullary electroreceptors detect relatively low-frequency electrical information.
source: All electroreceptive lineages (mormyroids, Xenomystus, gymnotiforms, and siluriforms) have evolved ampullary electroreceptors, which detect relatively low-frequency electrical information, while only gymnotiforms and mormyroids have evolved additional tuberous electroreceptors that broaden the frequency range of detectable signals (Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Only gymnotiforms and mormyroids have evolved additional tuberous electroreceptors.
source: All electroreceptive lineages (mormyroids, Xenomystus, gymnotiforms, and siluriforms) have evolved ampullary electroreceptors, which detect relatively low-frequency electrical information, while only gymnotiforms and mormyroids have evolved additional tuberous electroreceptors that broaden the frequency range of detectable signals (Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Tuberous electroreceptors broaden the frequency range of detectable signals.
source: All electroreceptive lineages (mormyroids, Xenomystus, gymnotiforms, and siluriforms) have evolved ampullary electroreceptors, which detect relatively low-frequency electrical information, while only gymnotiforms and mormyroids have evolved additional tuberous electroreceptors that broaden the frequency range of detectable signals (Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Electrogenic species with both electroreceptor types cluster distinctly from electrogenic fishes with only ampullary electroreceptors.
source: We find that electrogenic species with both electroreceptor types cluster distinctly from electrogenic fishes with only ampullary electroreceptors (Synodontis siluriforms).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: PC1 explained 92.02% of the variation in brain region volumes.
source: The first principal component (PC1) explained 92.02% of the variation in brain region volumes and is strongly correlated with total brain volume (ρ = –0.99, p<10–16).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: PC1 is strongly correlated with total brain volume.
source: The first principal component (PC1) explained 92.02% of the variation in brain region volumes and is strongly correlated with total brain volume (ρ = –0.99, p<10–16).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: PC2 explained 4.81% of the total variation, which is 60.3% of the variation in region volumes not explained by total brain volume.
source: PC2 explained 4.81% of the total variation, which is 60.3% of the variation in region volumes not explained by total brain volume.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: All brain regions loaded in the same direction for PC1.
source: Whereas all of the brain regions loaded in the same direction for PC1, cerebellum, torus semicircularis, and hindbrain loaded negatively on PC2 while the remaining regions (telencephalon, rest of brain, optic tectum, and olfactory bulbs) loaded positively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Cerebellum, torus semicircularis, and hindbrain loaded negatively on PC2.
source: Whereas all of the brain regions loaded in the same direction for PC1, cerebellum, torus semicircularis, and hindbrain loaded negatively on PC2 while the remaining regions (telencephalon, rest of brain, optic tectum, and olfactory bulbs) loaded positively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Telencephalon, rest of brain, optic tectum, and olfactory bulbs loaded positively on PC2.
source: Whereas all of the brain regions loaded in the same direction for PC1, cerebellum, torus semicircularis, and hindbrain loaded negatively on PC2 while the remaining regions (telencephalon, rest of brain, optic tectum, and olfactory bulbs) loaded positively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Concerted brain evolution explains the most variation in region volumes as seen in PC1.
source: This suggests that concerted brain evolution explains the most variation in region volumes as seen in PC1, but that mosaic brain evolution could be contributing to the observed variation in brain region volumes as seen in PC2.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section.

claim: Mosaic brain evolution could be contributing to the observed variation in brain region volumes as seen in PC2.
source: This suggests that concerted brain evolution explains the most variation in region volumes as seen in PC1, but that mosaic brain evolution could be contributing to the observed variation in brain region volumes as seen in PC2.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section.

claim: The model that considers the electrogenesis phenotype better explained PC1.
source: We found that the model that considers the electrogenesis phenotype better explained PC1, but is statistically indistinguishable from the concerted model (Figure 4—source data 2), which further supports the role of concerted evolution in determining the sizes of individual brain regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to source data.

claim: The model that considers electroreceptor type better explained PC2.
source: The model that considers electroreceptor type better explained PC2 (Figure 4—source data 2), which supports our hypothesis that the electrosensory system is related to mosaic evolutionary changes in brain region scaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to source data.

claim: There is a significant increase in y-intercept in cerebellum for all electrogenic species relative to non-electric species.
source: We found a significant increase in y-intercept in cerebellum for all electrogenic species relative to non-electric species (p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: There is a significant increase in y-intercept in torus semicircularis in electrogenic + ampullary-only taxa relative to non-electric taxa.
source: For torus semicircularis, we found a significant increase in y-intercept in electrogenic + ampullary-only taxa relative to non-electric taxa (p<0.05) and a further increase in y-intercept in electrogenic + ampullary + tuberous taxa (p<10–4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: There is a further increase in y-intercept in torus semicircularis in electrogenic + ampullary + tuberous taxa.
source: For torus semicircularis, we found a significant increase in y-intercept in electrogenic + ampullary-only taxa relative to non-electric taxa (p<0.05) and a further increase in y-intercept in electrogenic + ampullary + tuberous taxa (p<10–4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: There is a significant increase in y-intercept in hindbrain for electrogenic + ampullary + tuberous taxa relative to non-electric taxa.
source: We found a significant increase in y-intercept in hindbrain for electrogenic + ampullary + tuberous taxa relative to non-electric taxa (p<0.01) with electrogenic + ampullary-only taxa being intermediate (p>0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: There are significant decreases in y-intercept in olfactory bulbs and rest of brain for electrogenic + ampullary + tuberous taxa relative to both electrogenic + ampullary-only and non-electric taxa when regressed against total brain volume.
source: There were significant decreases in y-intercept in olfactory bulbs and rest of brain for electrogenic + ampullary + tuberous taxa relative to both electrogenic + ampullary-only and non-electric taxa when regressed against total brain volume (pOB<0.05, pRoB<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: There is a significant decrease in y-intercept in optic tectum in electrogenic + ampullary + tuberous taxa relative to non-electric taxa when regressed against total brain volume.
source: For optic tectum, we found a significant decrease in y-intercept in electrogenic + ampullary + tuberous taxa relative to non-electric taxa (p<10–4) with electrogenic + ampullary-only taxa as intermediate (p>0.05) when regressed against total brain volume.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: There are similar mosaic shifts in lineages that independently evolved electrogenesis regardless of analysis method.
source: These results show that there are similar mosaic shifts in lineages that independently evolved electrogenesis regardless of analysis method.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section.

claim: Mormyroids have a shallower slope and smaller y-intercept in olfactory bulbs compared to gymnotiforms when regressed against total brain volume.
source: When regressed against total brain volume, we found a shallower slope and smaller y-intercept for mormyroids in olfactory bulbs (pslope<10–4, pintercept<0.05) and rest of brain (pslope<10–2, pintercept<0.05), shallower slope for mormyroids in torus semicircularis (p<10–2), and steeper slope for mormyroids in cerebellum (p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Mormyroids have a shallower slope and smaller y-intercept in rest of brain compared to gymnotiforms when regressed against total brain volume.
source: When regressed against total brain volume, we found a shallower slope and smaller y-intercept for mormyroids in olfactory bulbs (pslope<10–4, pintercept<0.05) and rest of brain (pslope<10–2, pintercept<0.05), shallower slope for mormyroids in torus semicircularis (p<10–2), and steeper slope for mormyroids in cerebellum (p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Mormyroids have a shallower slope in torus semicircularis compared to gymnotiforms when regressed against total brain volume.
source: When regressed against total brain volume, we found a shallower slope and smaller y-intercept for mormyroids in olfactory bulbs (pslope<10–4, pintercept<0.05) and rest of brain (pslope<10–2, pintercept<0.05), shallower slope for mormyroids in torus semicircularis (p<10–2), and steeper slope for mormyroids in cerebellum (p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Mormyroids have a steeper slope in cerebellum compared to gymnotiforms when regressed against total brain volume.
source: When regressed against total brain volume, we found a shallower slope and smaller y-intercept for mormyroids in olfactory bulbs (pslope<10–4, pintercept<0.05) and rest of brain (pslope<10–2, pintercept<0.05), shallower slope for mormyroids in torus semicircularis (p<10–2), and steeper slope for mormyroids in cerebellum (p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: Non-electric osteoglossiforms have a significantly larger y-intercept for telencephalon compared to non-electric otophysans.
source: For non-electric fishes, we found that osteoglossiforms have a significantly larger y-intercept for telencephalon (pTEL<10–2), but no differences in either slope or y-intercept in the other brain regions (p>0.1) when regressed against both total brain volume (Figure 7B, Figure 7—source data 1) and remaining brain volume (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support and illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: There are no differences in either y-intercept or slope between wave and pulse gymnotiforms in any region against total brain volume.
source: However, we found no differences in either y-intercept or slope of any region against total brain volume between wave and pulse gymnotiforms and only a significant increase in slope in telencephalon against remaining brain volume for wave gymnotiforms (p<0.05), suggesting that the transition between discharge types did not relate to brain structure at this scale.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: The transition between discharge types did not relate to brain structure at this scale.
source: However, we found no differences in either y-intercept or slope of any region against total brain volume between wave and pulse gymnotiforms and only a significant increase in slope in telencephalon against remaining brain volume for wave gymnotiforms (p<0.05), suggesting that the transition between discharge types did not relate to brain structure at this scale.

evidence: This is stated with supporting citations and reference to Figure 3.

claim: When allowing only intercept to vary between grades while assuming parallel slopes, no reliable grade shifts within actinopterygians are detected.
source: Indeed, when we allow only intercept to vary between grades while assuming parallel slopes, we no longer detect any reliable grade shifts within actinopterygians.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Two of the identified shifts were undetectable when assuming the brain–body allometry is constant within orders.
source: Even when allowing slope to vary, two of our identified shifts were undetectable when assuming the brain–body allometry is constant within orders despite analyzing much of the same data (Tsuboi, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The study found differences in slope across region–brain allometries at varying taxonomic levels.
source: Like previous work in other lineages (Finlay and Darlington, 1995; Yopak et al., 2010), we also find differences in slope across region–brain allometries at varying taxonomic levels, indicating that the dramatic differences in observed region volumes can result from both mosaic shifts between lineages and evolutionary changes in total brain size within a lineage (Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Dramatic differences in observed region volumes can result from both mosaic shifts between lineages and evolutionary changes in total brain size within a lineage.
source: Like previous work in other lineages (Finlay and Darlington, 1995; Yopak et al., 2010), we also find differences in slope across region–brain allometries at varying taxonomic levels, indicating that the dramatic differences in observed region volumes can result from both mosaic shifts between lineages and evolutionary changes in total brain size within a lineage (Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: Interspecific (evolutionary) allometries are an emergent property of developmental (within individuals) and static (within species) allometries.
source: As interspecific (evolutionary) allometries are an emergent property of developmental (within individuals) and static (within species) allometries (Pélabon et al., 2014; Tsuboi, 2021), it is difficult to assess the mechanism leading to these differences in slope across species without further research into evolutionary changes in developmental and static allometries.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Evolutionary changes in both the static slope and intercept are contributing to the steeper evolutionary slope found across osteoglossiforms.
source: Previous work considering the effect of static allometries on evolutionary allometries found that evolutionary changes in both the static slope and intercept are contributing to the steeper evolutionary slope found across osteoglossiforms (Tsuboi, 2021).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Steeper static slopes may indicate a higher rate of brain growth to body growth in adult stages.
source: Steeper static slopes may indicate a higher rate of brain growth to body growth in adult stages while larger static intercepts might reflect increased brain mass at the transition between embryonic and juvenile growth phases in fishes (Oikawa et al., 1992; Oikawa and Itazawa, 1984; Tsuboi, 2021).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Larger static intercepts might reflect increased brain mass at the transition between embryonic and juvenile growth phases in fishes.
source: Steeper static slopes may indicate a higher rate of brain growth to body growth in adult stages while larger static intercepts might reflect increased brain mass at the transition between embryonic and juvenile growth phases in fishes (Oikawa et al., 1992; Oikawa and Itazawa, 1984; Tsuboi, 2021).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Previous work in marsupials did not find any mechanistic links between regional neurogenesis timing or growth rate and static or evolutionary region–brain allometric differences in either slope or intercept.
source: Previous work in marsupials did not find any mechanistic links between regional neurogenesis timing or growth rate and static or evolutionary region–brain allometric differences in either slope or intercept despite finding extensive heterochronic differences between species (Carlisle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The intraspecific mechanisms resulting in interspecific scaling differences may differ across species.
source: This finding suggests that the intraspecific mechanisms resulting in these interspecific scaling differences may differ across species, but additional research is needed to determine whether there are shared intraspecific mechanisms resulting in interspecific differences in slope versus intercept in other lineages, especially in those with extensive adult neurogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as an inference in the Discussion section.

claim: Different lineages can independently evolve the same phenotype via the same mechanism (parallel evolution) or different mechanisms (convergent evolution).
source: Different lineages can independently evolve the same phenotype via the same mechanism (parallel evolution) or different mechanisms (convergent evolution).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Discussion section.

claim: The study argues for a more conservative assumption of convergent evolution for electrosensory cerebrotypes.
source: Given the phylogenetic distance between osteoglossiforms and otophysans, it would be more remarkable to find that the different electrosensory systems and mosaic shifts in brain region volumes evolved in parallel rather than by convergence. Given that the mechanism of these regional increases remains unknown, we argue for a more conservative assumption of convergent evolution for electrosensory cerebrotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The cerebellar subregion that has expanded the most in mormyroids is the valvula cerebelli.
source: This is supported by the fact that the cerebellar subregion that has expanded the most in mormyroids is the valvula cerebelli while in gymnotiforms, it is the corpus cerebelli (Meek and Nieuwenhuys, 1998).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: In gymnotiforms, the cerebellar subregion that has expanded the most is the corpus cerebelli.
source: This is supported by the fact that the cerebellar subregion that has expanded the most in mormyroids is the valvula cerebelli while in gymnotiforms, it is the corpus cerebelli (Meek and Nieuwenhuys, 1998).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The torus is laminar in gymnotiforms.
source: Additionally, the torus is laminar in gymnotiforms while there are distinct nuclei in the non-laminar torus of mormyroids (Bell and Maler, 2005), and we find evidence of a steeper brain–body allometric relationship for osteoglossiforms that appears unrelated to the evolution of an electrosensory system in mormyroids.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: There are distinct nuclei in the non-laminar torus of mormyroids.
source: Additionally, the torus is laminar in gymnotiforms while there are distinct nuclei in the non-laminar torus of mormyroids (Bell and Maler, 2005), and we find evidence of a steeper brain–body allometric relationship for osteoglossiforms that appears unrelated to the evolution of an electrosensory system in mormyroids.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The study found evidence of a steeper brain–body allometric relationship for osteoglossiforms that appears unrelated to the evolution of an electrosensory system in mormyroids.
source: Additionally, the torus is laminar in gymnotiforms while there are distinct nuclei in the non-laminar torus of mormyroids (Bell and Maler, 2005), and we find evidence of a steeper brain–body allometric relationship for osteoglossiforms that appears unrelated to the evolution of an electrosensory system in mormyroids.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The study found a subsequent decrease in the brain–body allometry of two small-brained sister mormyroids (I. henryi and B. brachyistius).
source: Interestingly, we found a subsequent decrease in the brain–body allometry of two small-brained sister mormyroids (I. henryi and B. brachyistius), which further suggests the steeper brain–body allometry of osteoglossiforms is unrelated to electrosensory capabilities.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The study provides evidence of repeated, independent mosaic evolution of major brain regions in association with a convergent behavioral novelty.
source: Regardless of whether the mechanism of relative regional scaling evolution is convergent or parallel, we provide evidence of repeated, independent mosaic evolution of major brain regions in association with a convergent behavioral novelty.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: The findings demonstrate that evolutionary changes in gross-scale brain structure are surprisingly predictable alongside the evolution of active electrosensory systems.
source: These findings demonstrate that evolutionary changes in gross-scale brain structure are surprisingly predictable alongside the evolution of active electrosensory systems, even when the underlying brain–body allometry differs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: The findings suggest that mosaic brain evolution may occur alongside the evolution of behavioral novelty.
source: More broadly, these findings suggest that mosaic brain evolution may occur alongside the evolution of behavioral novelty and could reflect a degree of predictability in brain evolution with behavioral evolution, especially when constraint in brain–body allometries are strong.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: The study measured structural brain variation for 63 individuals from 22 species.
source: We measured structural brain variation for 63 individuals from 11 gymnotiform species, 7 siluriform species (4 from the electrogenic genus Synodontis), 2 characiform species, and 2 cypriniform species.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The study recorded electrical discharges from all three tested Synodontis species.
source: We recorded electrical discharges from all three tested species (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The confirmed electrogenic Synodontis spp. are broadly distributed throughout the species radiation.
source: Further, the confirmed electrogenic Synodontis spp. are broadly distributed throughout the species radiation (Day et al., 2013; Pinton et al., 2013), so additional research is needed to identify the number of origins and losses of electrogenesis among Synodontis fishes.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Synodontis catfishes would be a good place to study the intermediate relationships between evolutionary changes in brain structure and evolution of electrogenesis.
source: Given the apparent lability of electrogenesis in Synodontis catfishes, these fishes would be a good place to study the intermediate relationships between evolutionary changes in brain structure and evolution of electrogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The study used neuroanatomical landmarks based on previous neuroanatomical studies to consistently delineate brain regions.
source: We used neuroanatomical landmarks based on previous neuroanatomical studies (Abrahão et al., 2018; Loomis et al., 2019; Maler et al., 1991; Ullmann et al., 2010) to consistently delineate brain regions (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations and reference to Figure 9.

claim: The study transformed brain volumes to brain masses by multiplying the volume by the density of fixed brain tissue.
source: Prior to this analysis, we transformed brain volumes to brain masses by multiplying the volume by the density of fixed brain tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The mean fixed brain tissue density was 1.32 g/cm3 (SD = 0.19).
source: To determine the density of fixed brain tissue, brains from six individuals across three species were dissected and weighed immediately after scanning. We then calculated the mean fixed brain tissue density (1.32 g/cm3, SD = 0.19) for these individuals and estimated the corresponding mass for each of our remaining brain volumes using this mean fixed brain tissue density.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The study built a Bayesian phylogenetic tree from 6 aligned and concatenated genes of 189 species.
source: As all of our focal species were not present in the phylogeny used above, we built a Bayesian phylogenetic tree from 6 aligned and concatenated genes (16s, coI, cytb, rh1, rag1, and rag2) of 189 species spanning Anguilliformes to Ostariophysi using Beast v1.10.4 (Suchard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The study constrained the monophyly of each order, gymnotiform families, elopomorpha, ostariophysi, and gymnotiforms + siluriforms as sister to each other.
source: To reduce the computational burden and improve taxonomic resolution, we constrained the monophyly of each order, gymnotiform families, elopomorpha, ostariophysi, and gymnotiforms + siluriforms as sister to each other following previous studies that used substantially more sequence data and tested alternative hypotheses of teleost topology but did not include all of the species used in this study (Hughes et al., 2018; Rabosky et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations.

claim: The study's purpose was to correct for relatedness as best as possible, not to propose a resolved phylogeny.
source: Given the uncertainty of phylogenetic relationships both among otophysans and within gymnotiforms (Crampton, 2019; Hughes et al., 2018; Rabosky et al., 2013) and our use of relatively few previously sequenced genes, we make no claims that these are the actual phylogenetic relationships between these species. Instead, our purpose in this study was to correct for relatedness as best we could.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
